extraction.body: Police explained that the serious security threat to the Ella Langley show caused a major police response - the show had to be cancelled. Ella Langley cancelled her October 9 show in Tulsa, Oklahoma. The show was cancelled due to a "serious security threat", per Rolling Stone . She announced the troubling news in a post on social media. "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show," she wrote. The show, which was set to happen at the BOK Center , was cancelled just hours before doors were set to be open. She confirmed that "this decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team." Her announcement continued with a heartfelt apology for her fans. She explained that she knows "how much time, travel, money and planning goes into coming to a show... and I can't tell you how sorry I am." "This is not a decision that was made lightly," she continued. "I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way," her announcement concluded. Ella Langley also confirmed that information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible". Per NBC News , Tulsa police said on Friday night that "a call was made threatening the lives of people attending the event." They took the threat seriously, having deployed their K-9s, bomb team, and patrols in tandem with venue security. They swept the building a total of two times, and "found no credible threat to the event's safety". However, they decided to "cancel the performance anyway" just to err on the side of caution. Tulsa police also apologized to any Ella Langley fans who "came down tonight". "We appreciate your patience," they added. "It is unfortunate that some nefarious characters successfully disrupted the event, ruining the evening for thousands of people". The situation remains under investigation. If nothing else, we're glad that no-one was hurt. We hope that the rest of Ella Langley's tour isn't disrupted like this.

extraction.body: Country singer Ella Langley canceled her sold-out show slated for Friday evening in Tulsa, Oklahoma, due to what she described as “a serious security threat.” The 27-year-old star announced the last-minute cancellation on Instagram, saying the threat involved “the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team.” “The incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show,” she said. “This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team.” Tulsa police said Friday “a call was made threatening the lives of people attending the event.” Police swept the area with its K-9, bomb team, patrol and venue security but did not find anything dangerous, and the building and surrounding area was swept a second time but police “again found no credible threat to the event’s safety,” the department said. Police said that it advised Langley’s staff that no credible threat was found, “but they decided to cancel the performance anyway.” “We apologize to everyone who came down tonight. We appreciate your patience, and it is unfortunate that some nefarious characters successfully disrupted the event, ruining the evening for thousands of people,” police said. Langley — whose single “Choosin’ Texas” has made history for topping the Billboard Hot 100 for over 23 weeks — apologized to her fans, but stressed safety is paramount. “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. extraction.body: Country singer Ella Langley canceled her sold-out show slated for Friday evening in Tulsa, Oklahoma, due to what she described as “a serious security threat.” The 27-year-old star announced the last-minute cancellation on Instagram, saying the threat involved “the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team.” “The incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show,” she said. “This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team.” Tulsa police said Friday “a call was made threatening the lives of people attending the event.” Police swept the area with its K-9, bomb team, patrol and venue security but did not find anything dangerous, and the building and surrounding area was swept a second time but police “again found no credible threat to the event’s safety,” the department said. Police said that it advised Langley’s staff that no credible threat was found, “but they decided to cancel the performance anyway.” “We apologize to everyone who came down tonight. We appreciate your patience, and it is unfortunate that some nefarious characters successfully disrupted the event, ruining the evening for thousands of people,” police said. Langley — whose single “Choosin’ Texas” has made history for topping the Billboard Hot 100 for over 23 weeks — apologized to her fans, but stressed safety is paramount. “I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly,” she said. The show was set to take place at Tulsa’s BOK Center, which shared the same statement Langley included in her post on social media. “The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolutely priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed,” the statement said. “The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first.” The statement said details regarding refunds will be shared soon.

extraction.body: Tulsa police swept the BOK Center twice and found no credible threat. The country star says the decision was made with authorities, the venue and her security team. Ella Langley canceled her sold-out concert at the BOK Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma, on Friday, Oct. 9, just hours before showtime. Her team pointed to a “serious security threat.” Tulsa police say they searched the arena twice, found nothing and did not tell anyone to call the show off. The concert was a stop on Langley’s Dandelion Tour, with Kameron Marlowe and Laci Kaye Booth booked as openers. Officers did a routine sweep of the arena with bomb-detection dogs before the show, and the event was cleared to go ahead , ABC News reported. Later that day, someone called in a warning that “someone was going to do great harm” at the concert, with “shots fired and bombs,” according to Reuters . Police searched the building a second time and added officers around the venue. They didn’t find anything. Tulsa Police Captain Richard Meulenberg addressed it in a video on Facebook. He said officers told the performers “we could not find a credible threat,” and that the department did not advise canceling. “Everything is safe,” he said. Police believe the call was most likely a swatting attempt, KTUL reported . The FBI is helping with the investigation, and Tulsa Crime Stoppers is asking anyone with information to call 918-596-COPS. The cancellation went out just before 5 p.m. Central. In a statement with the BOK Center, Langley’s team said “the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority.” Langley posted her own message on social media. She said the call “was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team,” which doesn’t quite line up with what police said afterward. “This is not a decision that was made lightly,” she wrote . “I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” She apologized to the fans who had traveled and paid to see her and told them their “safety will always mean more to me than anything else.” The BOK Center said refund details “will be shared as soon as possible.” No make-up date had been announced as of Saturday morning. Langley is scheduled to play United Supermarkets Arena in Lubbock, Texas , on Saturday night, followed by two shows at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles. The tour ends Oct. 31 in St. Paul, Minnesota. It’s been a huge year for Langley. extraction.body: Ella Langley's Friday-night concert in Tulsa was canceled hours before showtime after a threatening call raised fears for concertgoers' safety. Police say the caller warned of violence involving gunfire and bombs, but subsequent searches uncovered no credible threat. The cancellation has left fans facing disappointment while investigators examine the warning that disrupted the evening. The "Choosin' Texas" singer had been scheduled to perform at the BOK Center on October 9. Langley and the venue announced that the show could not proceed, citing a serious security threat affecting fans, venue personnel, and the artist. Ticket-refund information would be provided as soon as possible, according to the announcement. Tulsa Police Captain Richard Meulenberg offered a more detailed account of what happened. Officers initially cleared the venue following a routine sweep with bomb-detection dogs. After the threatening call, police conducted another search and again found no credible threat. Meulenberg said his department did not recommend cancellation. That creates an important distinction between the public statements. Langley said the decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, venue officials, and her security team. Police described the final cancellation as a decision by the performers after officers communicated their findings. The available reporting does not resolve exactly how those discussions unfolded. Langley's message emphasized her unwillingness to risk anyone's safety. "I refuse to put anyone in harm's way," she told fans, while acknowledging the travel, expense, and planning involved in attending a concert. Her apology underscored the consequences of a last-minute cancellation for people who had arranged their evening around the performance. The absence of a credible threat during the searches does not answer who made the call or why. ABC News reported that the FBI was assisting with the investigation, with no further details provided about its involvement. Those unanswered questions remain central to understanding how the planned concert became a security incident. For now, the confirmed development is that a warning involving guns and bombs prompted additional police searches, followed by the cancellation. The concert was a stop on Langley’s Dandelion Tour, with Kameron Marlowe and Laci Kaye Booth booked as openers. Officers did a routine sweep of the arena with bomb-detection dogs before the show, and the event was cleared to go ahead , ABC News reported. Later that day, someone called in a warning that “someone was going to do great harm” at the concert, with “shots fired and bombs,” according to Reuters . Police searched the building a second time and added officers around the venue. They didn’t find anything. Tulsa Police Captain Richard Meulenberg addressed it in a video on Facebook. He said officers told the performers “we could not find a credible threat,” and that the department did not advise canceling. “Everything is safe,” he said. Police believe the call was most likely a swatting attempt, KTUL reported . The FBI is helping with the investigation, and Tulsa Crime Stoppers is asking anyone with information to call 918-596-COPS. The cancellation went out just before 5 p.m. Central. In a statement with the BOK Center, Langley’s team said “the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority.” Langley posted her own message on social media. She said the call “was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team,” which doesn’t quite line up with what police said afterward. “This is not a decision that was made lightly,” she wrote . “I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” She apologized to the fans who had traveled and paid to see her and told them their “safety will always mean more to me than anything else.” The BOK Center said refund details “will be shared as soon as possible.” No make-up date had been announced as of Saturday morning. Langley is scheduled to play United Supermarkets Arena in Lubbock, Texas , on Saturday night, followed by two shows at the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles. The tour ends Oct. 31 in St. Paul, Minnesota. It’s been a huge year for Langley. Her single “Choosin’ Texas” set a Billboard Hot 100 record in September for the most weeks at No. 1, passing Mariah Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” This article first appeared on Men's Journal and was syndicated with permission. Her apology underscored the consequences of a last-minute cancellation for people who had arranged their evening around the performance. The absence of a credible threat during the searches does not answer who made the call or why. ABC News reported that the FBI was assisting with the investigation, with no further details provided about its involvement. Whether it’s Waylon, Willie and legends of the past, or the superstars of today like Zach Bryan, our finger is always on the pulse of true country music. From Texas to Tennessee, Appalachia to Bakersfield, Whiskey Riff is THE unapologetic voice of the country music fan. A RIFF on what makes the great outdoors…great. “Country” is more than just a steel guitar. It’s a lifestyle, a mindset, and a way to speak your mind and not apologize for it. Whiskey Riff is that lifestyle. On ‘Whiskey Riff Raff’ buckle up for an unfiltered and unapologetic take on country music, life, sports, and all the craziness that comes with it. Laugh with us. Rant with us. Drink with us. This evening, Ella Langley was forced to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma slated for the BOK Center due to what is being described as “a serious security threat.” She says additional information, as well as refund information, will be shared as soon as possible: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled. The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concert and will always come first. Additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we prioritize the safety of all involved.” Ella shared the news in a post on Instagram, saying she is very, very sorry for having to do this, noting that she knows “much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show.” We all know it takes a lot, so I’m sure fans will understandably be disappointed, but safety always comes first. She added that the decision was not made lightly, and of course, there was a lot of input from local authorities as well as her own personal security team: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” I know she would never do this so last minute if it wasn’t very serious, and while there’s no word on what the specific threat is, the priority is her safety and the safety of all fans, and that will always be the most important thing, and I’m sure she will be back to make it up to her fans when it’s safe to do so. As we near the end of the year, it’s becoming increasingly clear that 2026 will go down as the year of Ella Langley. Simply put, it’s hard to argue that she’s not just the hottest star in country music, but as music as a whole. If you’ve been paying close attention within the genre over the years, it was more than apparent that the Alabama native was bound to be a star, catching early buzz with tracks like “Country Boy’s Dream Girl,” “paint the town blue” and “That’s Why We Fight” with Koe Wetzel. With that being said, however, I don’t think anyone could have predicted the world-dominating, record-smashing success she’s had recently. Launching off the success of her Riley Green collaboration, “you look like you love me” throughout 2024 and 2025, as well as other hits such as “weren’t for the wind,” the Alabama native has become nothing short of a phenomenon thanks to the megahit that is “Choosin’ Texas,” And, in turn, she has captured the hearts of nearly everyone in the country and the world over the past year. Since its release on October 17th, it is now the longest-running #1 hit by a female artist this century, the only country song by a woman to triple up and go #1 on Billboard’s Hot 100, Hot Country and Country Airplay charts simultaneously. In case that wasn’t enough, thanks to the success of her sophomore album, Dandelion, which debuted at #1 on the all-genre Billboard 200 and sold 169,000 equivalent album units in the U.S. in its first week, Langley became just the second woman in history to hold the #1 album and song in the U.S. simultaneously with a country song/album. Two weeks ago, she made U.S. history by officially capturing the longest-running #1 hit in U.S. history with 23 weeks (now 24), passing Mariah Carey’s long-standing record of 22 atop the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, and her record year continues as she adds more certifications and records to her catalog.

extraction.body: Country music is the lifeblood of Whiskey Riff, and we pride ourselves on standing firmly in the corner of the independent artists, and those few in the mainstream still doing it the right way. Whether it’s Waylon, Willie and legends of the past, or the superstars of today like Zach Bryan, our finger is always on the pulse of true country music. From Texas to Tennessee, Appalachia to Bakersfield, Whiskey Riff is THE unapologetic voice of the country music fan. A RIFF on what makes the great outdoors…great. “Country” is more than just a steel guitar. It’s a lifestyle, a mindset, and a way to speak your mind and not apologize for it. Whiskey Riff is that lifestyle. On ‘Whiskey Riff Raff’ buckle up for an unfiltered and unapologetic take on country music, life, sports, and all the craziness that comes with it. Laugh with us. Rant with us. Drink with us. This evening, Ella Langley was forced to cancel her concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma slated for the BOK Center due to what is being described as “a serious security threat.” She says additional information, as well as refund information, will be shared as soon as possible: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled. The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concert and will always come first. Additional information and details regarding ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. We appreciate your understanding and cooperation as we prioritize the safety of all involved.” Ella shared the news in a post on Instagram, saying she is very, very sorry for having to do this, noting that she knows “much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show.” We all know it takes a lot, so I’m sure fans will understandably be disappointed, but safety always comes first. She added that the decision was not made lightly, and of course, there was a lot of input from local authorities as well as her own personal security team: “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight’s show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am. This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way.” I know she would never do this so last minute if it wasn’t very serious, and while there’s no word on what the specific threat is, the priority is her safety and the safety of all fans, and that will always be the most important thing, and I’m sure she will be back to make it up to her fans when it’s safe to do so. As we near the end of the year, it’s becoming increasingly clear that 2026 will go down as the year of Ella Langley. Simply put, it’s hard to argue that she’s not just the hottest star in country music, but as music as a whole. If you’ve been paying close attention within the genre over the years, it was more than apparent that the Alabama native was bound to be a star, catching early buzz with tracks like “Country Boy’s Dream Girl,” “paint the town blue” and “That’s Why We Fight” with Koe Wetzel. With that being said, however, I don’t think anyone could have predicted the world-dominating, record-smashing success she’s had recently. Launching off the success of her Riley Green collaboration, “you look like you love me” throughout 2024 and 2025, as well as other hits such as “weren’t for the wind,” the Alabama native has become nothing short of a phenomenon thanks to the megahit that is “Choosin’ Texas,” And, in turn, she has captured the hearts of nearly everyone in the country and the world over the past year. Since its release on October 17th, it is now the longest-running #1 hit by a female artist this century, the only country song by a woman to triple up and go #1 on Billboard’s Hot 100, Hot Country and Country Airplay charts simultaneously. In case that wasn’t enough, thanks to the success of her sophomore album, Dandelion, which debuted at #1 on the all-genre Billboard 200 and sold 169,000 equivalent album units in the U.S. in its first week, Langley became just the second woman in history to hold the #1 album and song in the U.S. simultaneously with a country song/album. Two weeks ago, she made U.S. history by officially capturing the longest-running #1 hit in U.S. history with 23 weeks (now 24), passing Mariah Carey’s long-standing record of 22 atop the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, and her record year continues as she adds more certifications and records to her catalog.

Ella Langley and the BOK Center announced the cancellation on their official social media accounts Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, just before 5 p.m. Central Time. The announcement referred to a “serious security threat” involving the safety of fans, venue staff, and the artist. Richard Meulenberg explained that officers had already done a routine pre-concert sweep of the premises using bomb-detection dogs, which turned up nothing. But police later received a phone call warning that people at the event could be harmed by gunfire and bombs. “We came back out again with an overabundance of caution, used our bomb dogs again, searched the whole area,” Capt. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on the social platform X that her work helped make humanity’s first journeys to the moon possible. “To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement,” Olivier de Weck, the Apollo program professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and interim head of its aeronautics and astronautics department, told MIT News, a publication of the university's communications office. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.” In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said. “She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.” Hamilton graduated with a degree in mathematics from Earlham College in Richmond, Indiana, in 1958 and went to work for MIT in 1959. Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo. “She was a software engineer at a time when that field was in its infancy,” de Weck continued, “and she not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved.”

In recent years, a photo circulated online showing a smiling Hamilton, in her early 30s, standing next to a towering stack of pages containing codes her team used during the Apollo project. A Lego set celebrating the women of NASA that was unveiled in 2017 included a figure of Hamilton. And the marking in 2019 of the 50th anniversary of the Apollo 11 moon landing also brought attention, her daughter said.

“She definitely went from nobody knowing who she was to suddenly everyone knowing who she was, especially in her field,” Lauren Hamilton said. “And I think she was really happy to be acknowledged for what she did. But she was kind of a reserved person so the spotlight wasn’t necessarily a natural thing for her.”

Her early focus there included working with a meteorology professor on weather prediction software, according to the MIT News article. In the mid-1960s, she started at MIT's Instrumentation Lab, which had a NASA contract for Apollo.

After first working on software for uncrewed missions, she later led the team developing the onboard flight software for the crewed missions, and by 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the command and service module team, according to MIT News.
“We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s,” Hamilton told MIT News in 2009. “Coming up with solutions and new ideas was an adventure.”

“Because software was a mystery, a black box, upper management gave us total freedom and trust,” she continued. “We had to find a way, and we did. Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers.”
She worked at the Instrumentation Lab into the 1970s and then founded two software companies, according to MIT News.
Lauren Hamilton said her mother’s biggest interest was in the abstract. “She was very much a mathematician and into the abstraction of how to turn thought, I guess, into software,” she said.
She said her mother was also “a really eccentric and fun character” who loved collecting vintage clothing and had “a very mischievous sense of humor.”
“She encountered a lot of sexism in her field but she didn’t come back aggressively,” Lauren Hamilton said. “She would disarm people with her sense of humor or … just kind of dominate quietly.”
Born on Aug. 17, 1936, in Indiana, Hamilton grew up mostly in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, her daughter said, and she lived in Cambridge from when she was in her early 20s until her death.
Hamilton received many awards and accolades, including being awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, in 2016 by President Barack Obama.

passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

passages: Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering computer software engineer who led the development of on-board flight software for NASA’s Apollo moon missions, has died at age 90. According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Hamilton passed away on September 30, noting her decades-long influence on computing and spaceflight. Hamilton was the former head of the Software Engineering Division of MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory, where she led the development of the Apollo Guidance Computer’s onboard flight software.

By 1968, she was the assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. She later founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies, and authored more than 130 technical publications. In 2016, her contributions earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the highest honor for civilians in the United States, with President Barack Obama praising her role in shaping modern software engineering and enabling "giant leaps for humankind."Hamilton is survived by her family, daughter Lauren Hamilton, son-in-law Richard Selesnick, two grandsons, four great-grandchildren and her siblings John, David and Kathryn.
She joined MIT in 1959, initially writing weather-prediction software before moving into Project Apollo.

TWEET Software that helped save Apollo 11's Moon landing Hamilton's work proved particularly important during the historic Apollo 11 mission in 1969, when the Eagle lunar module was preparing to land on the Moon. According to NASA, approximately three minutes before touchdown, her software intervened to overcome a faulty script, allowing the mission to continue safely. Hamilton joined MIT in 1959, initially working in meteorology before moving into the Apollo project in 1965. She became the project's first programmer and first female programmer, eventually taking charge of major software development operations. By 1968, she had become assistant director responsible for the Apollo Command and Service Module software team, while more than 400 people were working on the program's software. NASA, MIT pay tribute to computing pioneer NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman paid tribute to Hamilton on X, describing her as a pioneer whose work made humanity's first lunar journeys possible. Olivier de Weck, interim head of MIT's Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, said that calling Hamilton ahead of her time would be an understatement, pointing to her leadership in developing one of the most complex technological systems ever undertaken. Jerry Wohletz, CEO of Draper Laboratory, which emerged from MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory, said Hamilton's contributions to the Apollo Guidance Computer helped astronauts reach the lunar surface and return safely to Earth. Hamilton received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of the United States' highest civilian honors, from then-President Barack Obama in 2016. TWEET Reflecting on the Apollo program in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton recalled the responsibility carried by the young engineers developing the software. We took our work seriously, many of us beginning this journey while still in our 20s," she said. "Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers," she added. Born in Indiana in 1936, Hamilton studied mathematics before moving to Boston with her husband in 1959. Beyond her work at NASA, she published more than 130 papers and founded two software companies, Higher Order Software and Hamilton Technologies.

extraction.body: TULSA, Okla. — The BOK Center announced country music singer Ella Langley's Friday night concert has been canceled due to a "serious security threat." The BOK Center released a statement that said in part, "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed. We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologize to fans who planned to attend. The safety of fans is our foremost concern and will always come first." FOX23 reached out to the Tulsa Police Department who said they believe the threat was likely a swatting call. According to TPD, officers carried out their regular security check they conduct before each concert and found nothing of concern. On Friday morning, authorities said they received a phone call threatening harm at the concert, though they said no details were specified by the caller. Following the call, the department said they conducted another security sweep of the venue and upped its security personnel at the BOK Center. TPD said they found no credible threat and believe there is no active threat at this time. The department said they did not advise either the BOK Center or Langley to cancel the concert, stating the decision to cancel the show was likely either made by the BOK Center itself or Langley's team. The BOK Center said information about ticket refunds will be shared as soon as possible. You can view the BOK Center's full statement below: The Tulsa Police Department released the following written and verbal statement addressing the situation: A sold-out concert was canceled tonight over threats of violence. Before the event, we swept the area with our K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol and BOK security for anything dangerous. Out of an abundance of caution, we swept the building and surrounding area and again found no credible threat to the event's safety. We advised the performer's staff that we found no credible threat to the event, but they decided to cancel the performance anyway. If you know anything about it that can be helpful and want a cash reward, call Tulsa Crime Stoppers at 918-596-COPS. Langley released the following statement on social media: "Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue and my security team. I refuse to put anyone in harm's way." KTUL will provide more information as it becomes available.

extraction.body: Country music star Ella Langley canceled a scheduled performance at Tulsa's BOK Center, citing a serious security threat. The decision was taken just hours before the show on Friday night (local time). Langley, 27, announced the cancellation on Instagram, expressing her regret and emphasizing that fan safety is her top priority. Langley wrote, Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team, the incredibly difficult decision was made to cancel tonight's show. She added, This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. Langley further said, I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can't tell you how sorry I am. According to local outlet News on 6, the concert was canceled due to a false bomb threat. The Tulsa Police Department stated that they found no credible threat after investigating the venue. They added that they had swept the area with their K-9, Bomb Team, Patrol, and BOK security for anything dangerous before the event. The BOK Center also confirmed the cancellation, stating that the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority. The incident is currently under investigation, and anyone with information has been asked to contact Tulsa Crime Stoppers.

HARDSIL helps reduce the design time and cost of developing new rad-hard products and can enhance the radiation tolerance of existing products without a redesign. With this acquisition, Microchip is positioned to capture a larger share of the A&D and space markets, which have seen accelerating investment and demand across both defense and commercial space programs. The transaction also strengthens Microchip’s technical capabilities through the addition of a team with deep radiation-hardening expertise that can be leveraged across the company’s broader business. extraction.body: CHANDLER, Ariz., Oct. 09, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Microchip Technology Incorporated (Nasdaq: MCHP), a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today announced that it has acquired VORAGO Technologies, Inc., a privately held provider of radiation-hardened and radiation-tolerant microcontrollers (MCUs) and microprocessors (MPUs), based in Austin, Texas. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed, and the acquisition is not expected to be material to Microchip's consolidated financial results. "From terrestrial defense systems to satellite and space-based platforms, our aerospace and defense customers are designing systems that must operate reliably in increasingly harsh and complex environments," said Steve Sanghi, Microchip's CEO and President. “The acquisition of VORAGO strengthens our ability to support development in these demanding markets and reinforces our commitment to investing in technologies that align with our long-term growth strategy.” The acquisition adds a family of radiation-hardened MCUs and MPUs that complement Microchip's existing aerospace and defense product lines, along with VORAGO's patented HARDSIL ® process technology. HARDSIL helps reduce the design time and cost of developing new rad-hard products and can enhance the radiation tolerance of existing products without a redesign. With this acquisition, Microchip is positioned to capture a larger share of the A&D and space markets, which have seen accelerating investment and demand across both defense and commercial space programs. The transaction also strengthens Microchip’s technical capabilities through the addition of a team with deep radiation-hardening expertise that can be leveraged across the company’s broader business. VORAGO's MCUs are designed to keep working where standard electronics fail, tolerating high radiation exposure and extreme heat, which makes them well suited for mission-critical space, defense and industrial applications. “VORAGO has always been focused on delivering the best radiation-protected semiconductor solutions that customers can depend on when failure is not an option. Joining Microchip gives us the opportunity to build on that foundation with greater scale, broader capabilities and the resources to serve a rapidly growing space market. I’m proud of what our team has built, and excited for how this acquisition can empower our customers to execute missions faster and with very high confidence,” said Bernd Lienhard, Chief Executive Officer of VORAGO Technologies. CHANDLER, Ariz., Oct. 09, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Microchip Technology Incorporated (Nasdaq: MCHP), a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today announced that it has acquired VORAGO Technologies, Inc., a privately held provider of radiation-hardened and radiation-tolerant microcontrollers (MCUs) and microprocessors (MPUs), based in Austin, Texas. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed, and the acquisition is not expected to be material to Microchip's consolidated financial results. "From terrestrial defense systems to satellite and space-based platforms, our aerospace and defense customers are designing systems that must operate reliably in increasingly harsh and complex environments," said Steve Sanghi, Microchip's CEO and President. “The acquisition of VORAGO strengthens our ability to support development in these demanding markets and reinforces our commitment to investing in technologies that align with our long-term growth strategy.” The acquisition adds a family of radiation-hardened MCUs and MPUs that complement Microchip's existing aerospace and defense product lines, along with VORAGO's patented HARDSIL ® process technology. HARDSIL helps reduce the design time and cost of developing new rad-hard products and can enhance the radiation tolerance of existing products without a redesign. With this acquisition, Microchip is positioned to capture a larger share of the A&D and space markets, which have seen accelerating investment and demand across both defense and commercial space programs. The transaction also strengthens Microchip’s technical capabilities through the addition of a team with deep radiation-hardening expertise that can be leveraged across the company’s broader business. VORAGO's MCUs are designed to keep working where standard electronics fail, tolerating high radiation exposure and extreme heat, which makes them well suited for mission-critical space, defense and industrial applications. “VORAGO has always been focused on delivering the best radiation-protected semiconductor solutions that customers can depend on when failure is not an option. Joining Microchip gives us the opportunity to build on that foundation with greater scale, broader capabilities and the resources to serve a rapidly growing space market. I’m proud of what our team has built, and excited for how this acquisition can empower our customers to execute missions faster and with very high confidence,” said Bernd Lienhard, Chief Executive Officer of VORAGO Technologies. Headquartered in Chandler, Arizona, Microchip offers outstanding technical support and delivers solutions across the industrial, automotive, consumer, aerospace and defense, communications and computing markets. For more information, visit the Microchip website at www.microchip.com . extraction.body: CHANDLER, Ariz., Oct. 09, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Microchip Technology Incorporated (Nasdaq: MCHP), a broadline supplier of semiconductors committed to making innovative design easier through total system solutions, today announced that it has acquired VORAGO Technologies, Inc., a privately held provider of radiation-hardened and radiation-tolerant microcontrollers (MCUs) and microprocessors (MPUs), based in Austin, Texas. Terms of the transaction were not disclosed, and the acquisition is not expected to be material to Microchip's consolidated financial results. "From terrestrial defense systems to satellite and space-based platforms, our aerospace and defense customers are designing systems that must operate reliably in increasingly harsh and complex environments," said Steve Sanghi, Microchip's CEO and President. “The acquisition of VORAGO strengthens our ability to support development in these demanding markets and reinforces our commitment to investing in technologies that align with our long-term growth strategy.” The acquisition adds a family of radiation-hardened MCUs and MPUs that complement Microchip's existing aerospace and defense product lines, along with VORAGO's patented HARDSIL ® process technology. HARDSIL helps reduce the design time and cost of developing new rad-hard products and can enhance the radiation tolerance of existing products without a redesign. With this acquisition, Microchip is positioned to capture a larger share of the A&D and space markets, which have seen accelerating investment and demand across both defense and commercial space programs. The transaction also strengthens Microchip’s technical capabilities through the addition of a team with deep radiation-hardening expertise that can be leveraged across the company’s broader business. VORAGO's MCUs are designed to keep working where standard electronics fail, tolerating high radiation exposure and extreme heat, which makes them well suited for mission-critical space, defense and industrial applications. “VORAGO has always been focused on delivering the best radiation-protected semiconductor solutions that customers can depend on when failure is not an option. Joining Microchip gives us the opportunity to build on that foundation with greater scale, broader capabilities and the resources to serve a rapidly growing space market. I’m proud of what our team has built, and excited for how this acquisition can empower our customers to execute missions faster and with very high confidence,” said Bernd Lienhard, Chief Executive Officer of VORAGO Technologies. passages: Country star Ella Langley's Tulsa, Oklahoma, show scheduled for Friday night has been abruptly canceled as a result of "a serious security threat." The venue, BOK Center, posted to social media Friday afternoon: "Due to a serious securty threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley's scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled." "The safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we determined that the show cannot proceed," the message added.

Langley herself took to her Instagram to apologize, telling fans that the "decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team." "I can't tell you how sorry I am," she wrote, acknowledging that she knows her fans took substantial "time, travel, money, and planning" to come to the show.
Last week at a show in Columbus, Ohio, Langley told the crowd , "I don't think I've ever had more opinions on myself in my life than I have in this last year."

Ella Langley was forced to abruptly cancel tonight’s concert (Oct. 9) at BOK Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as part of her Dandelion Tour due to a “serious security threat” involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist. Just a few hours before the show, BOK Center took to social media to announce the sudden cancellation in an “important show update,” explaining that the decision was made after careful consideration of the potential threat and the safety of everyone involved. “Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled,” the venue stated. sources.title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
passages: The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters.

Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

extraction.body: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck. The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor. Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago. Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees. Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market. “I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks. "“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck. “It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco. Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago. I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed. To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects. The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify.

extraction.body: Please login to add favorites. \n Dismiss this notice \n","authentication_redirect":"","dev_mode":"","logged_in":"","user_id":"0","authentication_redirect_url":"https:\/\/www.theautopian.com\/?memberful_endpoint=auth"}; /* */ Youtube Facebook-f Twitter Instagram Rss Sign in Register Menu Sign in Register Night Panel Disable Night Panel News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Menu News Reviews Merch Toys Tips Glovebox Become a Member Home » Watch Jay Leno Drive The Adorable Telo, A Mini Cooper-Sized Electric Truck That Promises F-150 Payload Watch Jay Leno Drive The Adorable Telo, A Mini Cooper-Sized Electric Truck That Promises F-150 Payload By Thomas Hundal April 28, 2025 3:42 pm 65 Comments It sure seems like pretty much all the exciting electric vehicle startups in America are focused on trucks. Rivian was the blueprint, but now Slate and Telo have each shown off radically different takes on the truck of the future. America’s car dad Jay Leno has driven the Telo MT1 prototype on a new episode of Jay Leno’s Garage , and the video’s given us some interesting extra tidbits of information about this Mini Cooper-sized crew cab pickup. To start, the truck uses off-the-shelf 2170 cells, the same size found in the Tesla Model 3, but Telo plans on building the 106 kWh battery packs in-house. It all should add up to a targeted curb weight of 4,400 pounds, which is pretty light for any crew cab truck. That’s less than what a Toyota Tacoma TRD Off Road weighs, and that thing’s still powered by combustion. Interestingly, Telo claims to have taken advice from the first Tesla-certified body shop in America on ways to reduce collision repair costs, such as tie rod placement. Moving to the body, Telo claims the production model will feature mechanical door handles, and the steering column will change for production as the makers of the truck aren’t quite happy with the tilt range. Interestingly, the Telo is homologated as an MPV, opening the door for future body styles, but a crew cab truck is it for now. It’s very cab-forward but it isn’t cab-over, as a look inside with the door open reveals that the driver sort-of goes around the wheel well. Speaking of construction, Telo claims that production body panels for the first 5,000 vehicles will be stamped using low-cost Kirksite tooling, a cast aluminum and zinc alloy that requires very little finishing to create an accurate die, but is mainly geared toward small-batch production. As for the bed, it measures 62 inches long with the divider up, 48 inches wide between the wheel wells, “about 60 inches” above the wheel wells. However, drop the rear seats, fold down the partition between the bed and the cab, and Telo claims you’ll be able to load a sheet of plywood flat with the tailgate up. While we’re back there, the Telo features a NACS port behind the tail light, and the release to access the charging port seems like it’s going to be mechanical, with a latch replacing the magnets holding the flap closed on the prototype. Oh, and we need to talk about the Rivian-style tunnel under the bed, because Telo has big plans for it. The company eventually wants to build a three-row SUV-style configuration on this platform, and use the tunnel as the footwell for third-row occupants. Leno’s actually taken the Telo MT1 prototype out for a spin, which is a pretty good basis on whether a vehicle from a new firm is real or not—if someone not employed by the company has driven the vehicle on public roads, there’s a good chance there’s something behind the effort that’s more than hype.This is a pre-production model built by Aria Group in California so it’s definitely not a finished product, but this early glimpse seems a bit noisy on the public roads. There’s plenty of motor noise audible in the video, and you can hear a few rattles, although those vibrations will probably be sorted by production. Speaking of production, it seems that Telo has modest plans for its sub-$50k truck. As Chief Technology Officer Forrest North told Leno, “We’re not trying to have aspirations of going high-volume manufacturing out of the gates. We want to build small-batch vehicles, small numbers, get them in customers’ hands, scale from there.” Perhaps that modest goal is why, unlike many EV startups, the production timeline for the first customer Telo MT1s has shifted up from 2026 to late 2025. The plan is to build these trucks in America, likely in California to start, so we’ll be watching closely to see where this goes. Rivian was the blueprint, but now Slate and Telo have each shown off radically different takes on the truck of the future. America’s car dad Jay Leno has driven the Telo MT1 prototype on a new episode of Jay Leno’s Garage , and the video’s given us some interesting extra tidbits of information about this Mini Cooper-sized crew cab pickup.

To start, the truck uses off-the-shelf 2170 cells, the same size found in the Tesla Model 3, but Telo plans on building the 106 kWh battery packs in-house. It all should add up to a targeted curb weight of 4,400 pounds, which is pretty light for any crew cab truck. That’s less than what a Toyota Tacoma TRD Off Road weighs, and that thing’s still powered by combustion. Interestingly, Telo claims to have taken advice from the first Tesla-certified body shop in America on ways to reduce collision repair costs, such as tie rod placement.

Moving to the body, Telo claims the production model will feature mechanical door handles, and the steering column will change for production as the makers of the truck aren’t quite happy with the tilt range. Interestingly, the Telo is homologated as an MPV, opening the door for future body styles, but a crew cab truck is it for now. It’s very cab-forward but it isn’t cab-over, as a look inside with the door open reveals that the driver sort-of goes around the wheel well. Speaking of construction, Telo claims that production body panels for the first 5,000 vehicles will be stamped using low-cost Kirksite tooling, a cast aluminum and zinc alloy that requires very little finishing to create an accurate die, but is mainly geared toward small-batch production.

As for the bed, it measures 62 inches long with the divider up, 48 inches wide between the wheel wells, “about 60 inches” above the wheel wells. However, drop the rear seats, fold down the partition between the bed and the cab, and Telo claims you’ll be able to load a sheet of plywood flat with the tailgate up. While we’re back there, the Telo features a NACS port behind the tail light, and the release to access the charging port seems like it’s going to be mechanical, with a latch replacing the magnets holding the flap closed on the prototype. Oh, and we need to talk about the Rivian-style tunnel under the bed, because Telo has big plans for it. The company eventually wants to build a three-row SUV-style configuration on this platform, and use the tunnel as the footwell for third-row occupants.

Leno’s actually taken the Telo MT1 prototype out for a spin, which is a pretty good basis on whether a vehicle from a new firm is real or not—if someone not employed by the company has driven the vehicle on public roads, there’s a good chance there’s something behind the effort that’s more than hype.This is a pre-production model built by Aria Group in California so it’s definitely not a finished product, but this early glimpse seems a bit noisy on the public roads. There’s plenty of motor noise audible in the video, and you can hear a few rattles, although those vibrations will probably be sorted by production.

Speaking of production, it seems that Telo has modest plans for its sub-$50k truck. As Chief Technology Officer Forrest North told Leno, “We’re not trying to have aspirations of going high-volume manufacturing out of the gates. We want to build small-batch vehicles, small numbers, get them in customers’ hands, scale from there.” Perhaps that modest goal is why, unlike many EV startups, the production timeline for the first customer Telo MT1s has shifted up from 2026 to late 2025. The plan is to build these trucks in America, likely in California to start, so we’ll be watching closely to see where this goes.

extraction.body: Telo claims its upcoming electric pickup will be able to tow more than originally planned. According to the startup, the MT1 EV will have a higher towing capacity than a base Ford F-150. The 152-inch pickup will also out-tow the base Tesla Cybetruck. Telo, the California startup that's trying to bring a small but powerful electric pickup truck to the market, now wants to play with the big boys when it comes to towing. Forrest North, the company's cofounder and chief technology officer, said in a YouTube video posted on Friday that the upcoming MT1 four-door pickup will be able to tow up to 8,000 pounds, up from the previously planned 6,600 pounds. That's a big number for such a small vehicle. As a reminder, Telo's first vehicle, which is not being mass-produced yet, is just 152 inches long—the same as the latest-generation Mini two-door hatchback. Despite that, it has four doors, it can seat up to five people, and has a 60-inch bed in the back. And now, with the increased towing capacity, the Telo MT1 is shaping up to be quite the urban worker—small enough to fit on small city streets, yet powerful enough to do big jobs. "In that 8,000 pound range, it unlocks the ability to have some of the new trailers that are coming onto the market which have active regen and battery packs of their own," North said. The video shows the Telo towing one such electrified camper, the Pebble Flow , which has a 45-kilowatt-hour battery pack, two hub motors, and a gross weight of 6,800 lbs. The company says the small truck can comfortably tow up to the new limit thanks to the regenerative braking capabilities of its electric motors. The fact that the vehicle itself weighs 4,400 lbs also helps keep it planted on the road, North said. Its bespoke electric platform has enabled designers and engineers to place the axles as close as possible to the car's front and rear, making more room for the cabin. That also enables the Telo to handle more weight on the tow hitch, North said, since the short distance between the rear axle and the tow hitch results in less levering force that would impact the front end. When it comes to towing, the base 2026 Ford F-150 with the 2.7-liter V6 EcoBoost engine and standard axle ratio can carry between 7,400 and 7,600 pounds. Meanwhile, the much more expensive Tesla Cybertruck Dual-Motor is rated for 7,500 lbs, all of which puts the diminutive Telo MT1 in a better place than anyone could've expected. (Both the F-150 and Cybertruck are also available in versions that can tow 11,000 lbs or more.) Telo claims an estimated starting MSRP of $41,520 for the entry-level model with a single rear electric motor and 260 miles of range. That's about $2,000 more than the cheapest F-150, which only has two doors, and about $2,000 more expensive than the most affordable four-door F-150. It's also $30,000 less than the base Cybertruck , though it's worth noting that Telo's plans also include a $50,000 model with dual-motor all-wheel drive and 350 miles of estimated range. All of this sounds pretty good, but right now, nobody can experience what Telo is claiming, except for its own employees. The startup is still working on getting its funky urban pickup into production. It recently announced a manufacturing contract with Schwab Industries, a Tier 1 automotive supplier, which will build its body-in-whites . Telo says production is slated to begin at the end of this year. coreStoryFacts.text: The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

extraction.body: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck. The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor. Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago. Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees. Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market. “I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks. "“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck. “It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco. Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago. I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed. To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects. The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. passages: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.
It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors.
The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ.

Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV.

Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds.
The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.
Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area.

The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters.
That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.
Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted.
It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.

"“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”" - Telo cofounder Forrest North Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles.
Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck.
Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup.
Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete.
They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck.
The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.
“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said.
At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range.
The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture.

The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.
Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house.
According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management.
Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing.
From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest.
With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed.

Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.
The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay.
How the Telo stacks up against the big trucks Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US.

Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify.
